summary: Reports on the Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale workshop held in Berlin in June 2015, which aimed to improve awareness and coordination among organizations responding to attacks. It is a report, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A meeting where people who fight online attacks got together to talk about how to work as a team.

questions: how do organizations coordinate on cyberattack response
what are barriers to sharing attack information
subtitle: Report on coordinating attack response at Internet scale

tldr.problem: Organizations responding to cyberattacks often work in isolation, and there is little coordination between incident response teams, vendors, service providers, and infrastructure operators despite the Internet-wide nature of modern threats.
tldr.mechanism: The CARIS workshop brought together approximately 50 representatives from CSIRTs, attack-response organizations, infrastructure providers, researchers, and vendors to discuss coordination challenges in real time, including trust, data sharing, DDoS response, and information exchange.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified recurring themes, barriers to coordination, and next steps for improving attack response at Internet scale, including better use of existing resources, improved communication protocols, and deeper collaboration between traditionally siloed communities.

today: RFC 8073 is an IAB Informational report documenting workshop consensus and recommendations. It remains a reference for understanding coordination challenges in large-scale incident response and has influenced subsequent work in standardization efforts such as the IETF DOTS, I2NSF, and MILE working groups.

sections.title: The CARIS Workshop and Its Goals
sections.content:
The Internet Architecture Board (IAB) and the Internet Society (ISOC) hosted a one-day workshop called Coordinating Attack Response at Internet Scale (CARIS) on June 18, 2015, in Berlin during the FIRST (Forum for Incident Response and Security Teams) Conference. The workshop brought together approximately 50 participants representing Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs), attack-response working groups, network and security operators, Regional Internet Registry (RIR) representatives, researchers, vendors, and representatives from standardization communities.

The primary goals were to improve mutual awareness, understanding, and coordination among diverse participating organizations, to increase awareness of existing mitigation efforts, and to foster collaboration between communities that typically work in isolation. The workshop was run under the Chatham House Rule to facilitate candid discussion of sensitive incident response topics.
sections.plainLanguage: A mix of security experts, operators, and vendors from different countries and organizations met in Berlin to discuss how to fight Internet attacks together better.

sections.title: Workshop Sessions: CSIRT Coordination and Information Exchange
sections.content:
The workshop included five panel sessions. The first addressed coordination between CSIRTs and attack-response mitigation efforts, examining how different organizations like ENISA, the Anti-Phishing Working Group (APWG), Ren-ISAC, CERT.br, MyCERT, and CERT/CC each approach incident response. Key insights included that organizations often focus on consuming threat data rather than sharing it, that ego and reputation concerns hinder data sharing, and that sharing must lead to operational improvements, not just create redundant blacklists.

A recurring finding was that operationally focused groups that successfully exchange data typically do so in small, trusted circles where personal relationships matter more than formal policies. Information sharing works best when organizations can quickly turn shared data into action to improve security, not simply to block attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Different security teams explained how they work, where they focus effort, and whether they share information with others. The teams found that data sharing works best when there is trust and when it helps them actually fix problems.

sections.title: DDoS, Botnets, and Infrastructure Coordination
sections.content:
The second session focused on scaling response to DDoS and botnets. The discussion noted that DDoS and botnet response are further along in efficient and effective mitigation than other attack types, but there is limited interaction between teams responding to these two threats even though botnets are often the source of DDoS attacks. Participants identified ad hoc trust groups like the Cybercrime Response Advisory Group (CRAG) within the operations security (OPSEC) community.

The third session examined how DNS providers and Regional Internet Registries could better collaborate with attack responders. RIRs maintain valuable datasets including worldwide BGP updates and root DNS server data that could benefit attack response, but the current data-sharing mechanisms do not scale well. Panelists noted that RIRs anonymize shared data and already coordinate with incident responders in their regions, suggesting opportunity for deeper engagement.
sections.plainLanguage: DDoS attacks and botnets can be fought well by some groups, but those groups do not always talk to each other. Infrastructure organizations like RIRs have useful information but need to share it in ways that scale better.

sections.title: Trust, Privacy, and Data-Sharing Barriers
sections.content:
A major theme across sessions was the challenge of trust and privacy in sharing sensitive incident data. Barriers to data sharing include privacy regulations, legal concerns, proprietary data sensitivity, cultural factors, and fear of appearing weak by admitting attacks. However, operationally focused groups found that many of these barriers are overstated when data sharing leads to concrete improvements.

Trust is personal rather than organizational: when sharing circles grow too large, trust breaks down. Successful sharing groups foster relationships between individuals through regular interaction and even social events. Some automation efforts found that people have different upper limits for trust group size, often based on individualized knowledge of other participants. Privacy regulations and the difficulty of identifying what constitutes personally identifiable information in aggregate also complicate automated data exchanges across regions.
sections.plainLanguage: People worry about sharing attack information because of privacy, competition, and fear of looking bad. But teams that actually share information say it works better when there is trust and it helps them.

sections.title: Key Themes and Next Steps
sections.content:
Two major themes emerged: First, data exchange should not merely create redundant blacklists but should support operational mitigation and elimination of vulnerabilities. Second, involving service providers and vendors is key to better scaling attack response, as security analysts are a scarce resource that should be leveraged through automation and better tools.

Recommended next steps included: expanding access to RIR and DNS provider resources with better documentation; improving education on basic security principles like ingress and egress filtering already documented in existing RFCs; developing better transport protocols for information exchange, including work in the IETF DOTS working group and XMPP-based protocols; and updating templates for documenting information exchange group capabilities to create a living library hosted by ISOC.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop concluded that sharing should lead to actually fixing problems, not just blocking attacks, and that better tools and protocols are needed for teams to exchange information at scale.
